title: Hardware Support
subtitle: Climb the money ladder -- one hardware question per grade level

gradeLabels.f: F-RANK -- Back to the Anti-Static Bag

questions.q: What is the primary job of a PSU (power supply unit) in a desktop PC?
options: It stores the system clock settings when the PC is off
It converts wall AC power into the DC voltages the PC needs
It regulates airflow to keep the CPU cool
It provides the clock signal to the CPU and RAM
questions.note: A PSU converts 120/240V AC from the wall into +12V, +5V, and +3.3V DC rails. The +12V rail powers the CPU and GPU.

explain.correct: The PSU is a power converter. It takes 120 V or 240 V AC from the wall outlet and outputs regulated DC rails: +12 V (CPU/GPU), +5 V, and +3.3 V. Without it, no component gets power.
wrong: That job belongs to the CMOS battery on the motherboard, which keeps BIOS settings and the real-time clock alive when the PC is unplugged.
Airflow is managed by case fans, the CPU cooler, and GPU fans -- not the PSU (though the PSU has its own fan to cool itself).
The system clock signal is generated by a crystal oscillator on the motherboard, not the PSU.

questions.q: Which video output port carries BOTH video AND audio signals over a single cable?
questions.note: HDMI and DisplayPort both carry video and audio. VGA and DVI carry video only -- neither has an audio channel.

explain.correct: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) was designed from the start to carry both high-definition video and multi-channel digital audio over one cable. DisplayPort also carries audio, but it is not one of the listed options.
wrong: VGA (Video Graphics Array) is an analog standard that carries video only. It has no audio channel, so a separate audio cable is always required.
DVI (Digital Visual Interface) carries video only. Even though DVI-I supports analog output, no DVI variant includes an audio channel.
PS/2 is a legacy keyboard and mouse port. It carries no video or audio -- it is a serial input interface.

questions.q: Where does a desktop RAM stick physically install?
options: A PCIe slot on the motherboard
An M.2 slot on the motherboard
A DIMM slot on the motherboard
A SATA port on the motherboard
questions.note: Desktop RAM uses full-size DIMMs (Dual In-line Memory Modules). Laptops use the smaller SO-DIMM. PCIe = expansion cards, M.2 = SSDs, SATA = drives.

explain.correct: Desktop DDR4/DDR5 RAM sticks are called DIMMs (Dual In-line Memory Modules) and install in long DIMM slots on the motherboard, typically two or four slots near the CPU socket.
wrong: PCIe slots hold expansion cards such as GPUs, network cards, and add-in NVMe cards -- not RAM sticks. They are keyed and shaped completely differently.
M.2 slots are thin, single-stick connectors used for M.2 SSDs (and some Wi-Fi cards). They do not accept RAM.
SATA ports are L-shaped 7-pin connectors for SATA hard drives and SSDs. RAM does not use SATA.

questions.q: Which storage option is fastest and most appropriate for a modern PC boot drive?
questions.note: Gen4 NVMe M.2 SSDs reach roughly 7000 MB/s sequential read. SATA SSDs top out near 550 MB/s. HDDs typically hit 100-200 MB/s.

explain.correct: NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) M.2 SSDs connect via PCIe lanes directly to the CPU, bypassing the older SATA bus. PCIe Gen 4 NVMe drives reach ~7000 MB/s sequential read vs ~550 MB/s for SATA SSDs and ~100-200 MB/s for HDDs.
wrong: A 7200 RPM HDD uses spinning magnetic platters and a mechanical read/write head. Sequential speeds are roughly 100-200 MB/s, and random access latency is high -- far slower than any SSD for boot workloads.
A SATA SSD is much faster than an HDD but is still limited by the SATA III interface to roughly 550 MB/s. It is a good upgrade but not the fastest option available.
An optical drive reads/writes discs (CD, DVD, Blu-ray). Sequential speeds are typically under 50 MB/s and optical drives are rarely used as boot media in modern builds.

questions.q: A PC powers on but always shows the wrong date and time, and you see a 'CMOS checksum error' message at POST. What is the most likely cause?
options: The GPU has failed and is outputting incorrect data
A RAM stick is faulty and corrupting the BIOS
The CMOS battery on the motherboard is dead
The PSU is under-voltage on the +3.3 V rail
questions.note: The CR2032 CMOS battery keeps BIOS settings and the real-time clock powered when the PC is off. When it dies, those settings -- including the date/time -- reset to defaults each boot.

explain.correct: The CMOS battery (typically a CR2032 coin cell) maintains BIOS configuration and the real-time clock when the PC is unplugged. A dead battery lets those values bleed away, so at POST the BIOS detects the mismatch between the stored and actual checksum and reports a 'CMOS checksum error'. The fix is replacing the coin cell.
wrong: A GPU failure causes display problems (artifacts, no signal, crashes under load) -- not BIOS checksum errors or clock resets. The GPU does not touch CMOS storage.
Faulty RAM typically causes POST beep codes, blue screens, or random reboots -- not repeated clock resets across power cycles. RAM does not store CMOS configuration.
A +3.3 V rail problem would likely cause broader instability or failure to POST at all. Isolated CMOS/clock issues without other symptoms point squarely at the CMOS battery.

questions.q: Intel's LGA (Land Grid Array) CPU socket design places the pins in which location?
options: On the CPU die itself, along the bottom edge
On the motherboard socket, protruding upward to contact the CPU
On the RAM module, bridging CPU and memory
LGA sockets have no pins; they use solder balls instead
questions.note: LGA = Land Grid Array. The socket on the motherboard has the pins; the CPU has flat metal lands (pads). AMD AM4 uses PGA (pins on the CPU). AMD AM5 switched to LGA like Intel.

explain.correct: In an LGA socket the delicate spring-loaded pins sit in the motherboard socket and make contact with flat metal pads (called 'lands') on the bottom of the CPU. This protects the CPU from bent-pin damage at the cost of more careful motherboard handling. Intel has used LGA since LGA775.
wrong: That describes PGA (Pin Grid Array), which AMD used for AM4 (Ryzen 1000-5000). In PGA the CPU has the pins and the motherboard socket has the holes. Intel abandoned PGA long ago.
RAM modules connect to DIMM slots and have no role in CPU socket pin design. The CPU-to-socket interface is entirely separate from the memory interface.

Solder-ball connections are used in BGA (Ball Grid Array) packaging, which is common in mobile/laptop CPUs that are soldered directly to the board. Desktop LGA and PGA sockets are socketed, not soldered.

questions.q: Which RAID level mirrors data across two drives, survives a single drive failure, and leaves you with 50 percent of total raw capacity as usable space?
questions.note: RAID 1 writes identical data to two drives (mirroring). With two 1 TB drives you get 1 TB usable. RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy; RAID 5 uses distributed parity; RAID 6 uses dual parity.

explain.correct: RAID 1 (mirroring) writes every block to both drives simultaneously. If one drive dies the other has a complete copy and the array keeps running. With N drives of equal size you get only one drive's worth of usable capacity -- 50 percent for a two-drive pair. It is the simplest redundancy scheme and requires a minimum of two drives.
wrong: RAID 0 stripes data across drives for increased performance but has ZERO redundancy. Losing a single drive destroys the entire array. It is the opposite of mirroring.
RAID 5 uses striping with distributed parity across a minimum of three drives. It survives one drive failure and gives N-1 usable capacity -- three drives of four, for example. It is not mirroring.

RAID 6 uses dual distributed parity across a minimum of four drives and can survive two simultaneous drive failures, giving N-2 usable capacity. It is more resilient than RAID 5 but uses more parity overhead.

questions.q: Which NAND flash type packs the MOST bits per cell, giving it the highest density and lowest cost per gigabyte, but also the LOWEST write endurance?
questions.note: SLC = 1 bit/cell (most durable, most expensive). MLC = 2 bits. TLC = 3 bits. QLC = 4 bits per cell (densest, cheapest, lowest P/E cycle endurance -- typically 100-1000 P/E cycles vs 100K for SLC).

explain.correct: QLC (Quad-Level Cell) stores four bits per cell by distinguishing 16 voltage states. This maximizes density and minimizes cost per GB but compresses the voltage window between states, making the cells far more sensitive to wear. QLC endurance is typically 100-1000 program/erase cycles, far below TLC (~1000-3000), MLC (~3000-10000), and SLC (~100000).
wrong: SLC stores only 1 bit per cell, giving it wide voltage margins, the highest endurance (~100000 P/E cycles), and the highest cost per GB. It is the most durable NAND type, not the least.
MLC stores 2 bits per cell. It is more durable than TLC and QLC and less expensive than SLC, sitting in the middle of the cost/endurance spectrum.
TLC stores 3 bits per cell and is the most common type in mainstream consumer SSDs. It has lower endurance than SLC and MLC but is more durable than QLC.

questions.q: Which UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) topology runs all power continuously through its battery and inverter, providing ZERO switchover time during an outage?
questions.note: Online double-conversion: AC in -> rectifier -> DC battery -> inverter -> AC out. Power always flows through the battery/inverter, so there is no transfer gap on outage. The most expensive and cleanest UPS type.

explain.correct: An online (double-conversion) UPS converts incoming AC to DC to charge the battery, then immediately inverts that DC back to clean AC for the load -- at all times, not just during an outage. Because power always flows through the inverter, there is literally zero milliseconds of switchover time when utility power fails. This also isolates connected equipment from all incoming power quality issues.
wrong: A standby (offline) UPS normally passes utility power straight through to the load and only switches to battery/inverter when it detects an outage. That transfer takes a few milliseconds (typically 2-10 ms), which is enough to cause a brief interruption for sensitive equipment.

A line-interactive UPS adds an automatic voltage regulator (AVR) to handle brownouts and over-voltages without switching to battery, but it still switches to battery on a full outage with a short transfer time (typically 2-4 ms). It is better than standby but not zero-switchover.

A surge protector is a passive device that clamps voltage spikes using MOVs (metal oxide varistors). It provides no battery backup whatsoever -- if power fails, everything connected to it loses power immediately.

questions.q: In a 4-drive RAID 5 array where each drive is 2 TB, how much total space is available for storing data?
questions.note: RAID 5 usable capacity = (N-1) x drive size. With 4 drives at 2 TB each: (4-1) x 2 TB = 6 TB usable. One drive's worth of space is consumed by distributed parity.

explain.correct: RAID 5 distributes parity stripes across all drives so that the equivalent of one drive's worth of space is used for parity. With N drives, usable capacity is (N-1) drives. For four 2 TB drives: (4-1) x 2 TB = 6 TB. The array can survive one drive failure; the parity blocks allow full reconstruction of the lost drive.
wrong: 8 TB would be the raw total of all four drives with no overhead -- that describes RAID 0 (striping with no parity). RAID 5 always sacrifices one drive's worth of space for parity.
4 TB (two drives' worth) is the usable capacity of RAID 6, which reserves the equivalent of two drives for dual parity. RAID 5 uses only one drive's worth of parity.
2 TB (one drive's worth) is the usable capacity of RAID 1 mirroring across two drives (or a RAID 1 pair). RAID 5 with four drives is much more space-efficient.

questions.q: A laser printer produces pages where the toner image is visible but smears or rubs off when touched. Every other function appears normal. Which component has most likely failed?
questions.note: The laser printing process order: charge, expose, develop, transfer, FUSE, clean. The fuser applies heat (~200 C) and pressure to melt toner permanently onto the paper. If it fails, toner sits loose on the surface and smears.

explain.correct: The fuser assembly is a heat-and-pressure station (typically a heated roller pressed against a pressure roller) that melts the toner particles into the paper fibers at roughly 180-220 degrees Celsius. Toner is essentially a fine plastic powder; without sufficient heat it never bonds and remains loose on the surface, smearing at the slightest touch. A fuser that is not reaching temperature -- due to a failed heating element, thermistor, or fuser lamp -- is the classic cause of this exact symptom.
wrong: The OPC drum (organic photoconductor) is a light-sensitive cylinder. The laser discharges it in the pattern of the image, attracting toner in the develop stage. A failed drum causes print quality defects like missing lines, solid black pages, or repeating marks at drum-circumference intervals -- not toner that rubs off. The toner would not even make it onto the paper correctly if the drum failed.

The transfer roller (or transfer belt in color printers) electrostatically moves the toner image from the drum surface to the paper. If the transfer roller fails, toner either stays on the drum (blank or faded pages) or transfers unevenly (streaks, ghosting). A transfer problem happens before the fuser stage; if toner is clearly visible but loose, transfer succeeded and the fuser failed.

The pickup roller feeds individual sheets from the paper tray into the paper path. If it fails, the printer either fails to pick up paper (paper jam at tray, 'paper empty' error) or picks up multiple sheets at once. It plays no role in toner adhesion.
